context: factory · long production lines; forming and welding or extrusion, testing and coating

brief.intro: New to this project type? A pipe factory is a long hall with one or more straight production lines. A steel pipe line uncoils strip or plate, forms it into a tube (spirally, or lengthwise), welds the seam, cuts the pipe to length, tests every pipe with water pressure and ultrasound or X-ray, and often coats it inside and out. A plastic (HDPE or PVC) pipe line melts pellets in an extruder, pushes them through a die, sizes and cools the pipe in long vacuum and water tanks, pulls it, cuts it and coils or stacks it. The buildings are simple; the lines are long, need accurate floors and foundations, a lot of power and cooling water, and outdoor space as large as the hall to store pipe.

glossary.plain: two ways of welding steel pipe seams: submerged-arc welding, or electric-resistance welding.
pipe formed by winding steel strip in a spiral and welding the seam.
the machine that melts plastic pellets and pushes the melt through a die to form pipe.
the vacuum tank that sizes the hot plastic pipe to its exact diameter.
the caterpillar unit that pulls the pipe through the line at a steady speed.
the machine that fills each pipe with water and holds it at test pressure.
factory-applied external coatings that protect steel pipe from corrosion.
the formal tests that prove the product meets its standard before it can be sold.

must_get_right: Layout first: line length, crane coverage and material flow decide the building; get the line supplier's general arrangement before designing the hall.
Cooling water and power are large — size and schedule the chillers, cooling towers and transformers with the lines, not after.
The pipe yard is part of the factory: paving, racks and lifting equipment must be ready for first production.
Product qualification and third-party certification come after the first pipes and can take weeks; sales cannot start before them.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by plant area along the process line and by discipline, with every long-lead machine tracked from order to factory test, shipping and arrival.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar for construction; equipment installation may run extended shifts under vendor supervision. Commissioning follows the vendor's programme, and hot commissioning runs continuously once started.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Supplier layout → foundations and long line floors → building and cranes → line installation and alignment → cooling water, power and air → dry runs → first pipes → qualification and certification. The critical path runs through the production-line delivery, then certification.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The process technology and vendor are fixed before design starts; vendor drawings for foundations arrive on the agreed dates; permanent power and water are available before cold commissioning; raw material for trial production is on site.

sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy machines need crane access and often must enter before the cladding or a wall is closed. Vendor supervisors are booked for fixed periods. Clean, dry, powered conditions are required before precision equipment is unpacked.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: late line delivery, floor and foundation tolerances, insufficient cooling or power at start-up, and failed qualification tests. Contingency is held before first certified production.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by plant area and discipline; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the installation crews and the vendor supervisors — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
